what_it_does: A spiking neural network (SNN) is a type of artificial neural network inspired by how biological neurons work: instead of passing continuous numbers between layers, neurons send discrete on/off pulses (spikes), which is inherently sparse and energy-efficient on neuromorphic hardware. As SNN architectures grow more complex to handle harder tasks, their energy advantage shrinks. This paper addresses that by aggressively pruning SNNs — removing unimportant connections and suppressing unnecessary spikes — across multiple dimensions at once. The key innovation is a dynamic joint pruning framework that simultaneously controls how often neurons fire (by learning firing thresholds), how much each time-step of activity matters (via a learnable time-scaling normalization layer), and which connections to keep (by tracking the real computational cost, measured as the number of synaptic operations, of each part of the network and pruning those with lowest impact). All three pruning dimensions are adjusted together during training rather than in separate stages.
